caption_en: 31. Cubicle (c), S wall, central section, central painting with Helen and Paris. The well-known subject of seduction, represented several times in vase painting since the fifth century BC, is found in Pompeian painting in two redactions (in which the positions, standing or sitting, of the two protagonists are reversed), with variations, within each of them, in the number of characters, in their arrangement and in their clothing. Here the standing hero is naked, with the chlamys gathered behind the body and on the left arm; he is characterized as a Phrygian by a barely hinted cap and leans, in a pose dating back to Polycletean models, on the arch he holds in his left. Helen sits in front of him, assisted by Aphrodite who reveals her nature in the attribute of the fan and in the jewels she wears; an erote, who in the Pompeian painter's interpretation replaces Himeros with the neo-Attic reliefs of a similar subject, flies behind the left shoulder of the goddess and with one hand attracts the hero towards the women. The scene, placed within a domestic environment, beyond the back walls of which a column can be seen, is well distributed in the almost square field of the painting and captures not the action but the state of mind of the characters, denoting, like that of a painting from Stabia (Museo Naz. di Napoli 8982) with the identical arrangement of the two protagonists,  to derive from a cartoon dating back to a Hellenistic model which, however, is also the basis of the other paintings of the same subject but with smaller characters, arranged upside down or paratactically.

1. Graphic reconstruction of the façade, with the cenacle consisting of tuff semi-columns on the first floor. It does not extend over the entire width of the façade; behind the N section (on the right) is the latrine on the first floor.

2. Atrium (A), wall N with the stairwell (left) and the built-in wardrobe set up under the stairs (right). The panels of the white plinth are separated by a narrow compartment with a plant; the white middle area consists of two panels bordered by a border of a staple carpet, bearing a figurative painting. The staircase went up to the wooden hallway that connected the rooms located on the first floor.

3. Atrium (A), wall N: stairwell, wall N. The plinth with a white background is adorned with a small picture flanked by a horizontal stretched garland. The white panel in the middle area, bordered by a border of a triangle carpet, bore a picture of which the lower left corner remains. 77 N34786

21. Tablinum (4), S section, floor and plinth of the S wall. The cocciopesto floor is dotted with large white tesserae arranged in parallel rows, according to the custom of the second century BC: it therefore probably dates back to the construction phase of the testudinate atrium (A).

The side panels of the plinth are adorned with a medallion in the center of a rhombus bordered by stretched garlands; The painting in the side panels of the middle area, bordered by edges of carpet with staples, depicts a still life (now illegible).

24. Tablinum (4), hall, W wall, section S, middle area, detail: candelabrum with garlands and birds perched on branches, which delimits the room on the side of the antechamber.

Cubicle (12), N wall, central section, middle area, detail: painting depicting Narcissus reflected in the water below the rock on which he is seated naked with a spear in his right hand, his red cloak thrown around his left leg. The oblique position of the hunter underlined by the weapon almost diagonally, is matched by the nymph Echo standing with her right hand resting on a pillar behind the rock; she wears a yellow chiton and a pale blue cloak. Note the quick but incisive brush of the painter of the paintings and panels with cupids in the cubicle that unfolds thin lines above the masses of bodies and clothes to structure the volumes (folds, facial features, hair, etc.). The same painter also apparently executed the Nilotic frieze in the garden.
80. Cubicle (12), entrance wall E, lunette. The white lunette is adorned with a sea griffin and green dolphins, which move in the direction of the door.

81. Cubicle (12), vault seen from E. The white vault presents, in the center, a gorgoneìon enclosed in a square placed at an angle, inscribed in a circle consisting of a garland inscribed in turn in a square with two concave sides, which accentuate the curve of the vault. In the resulting pendentives between the circle and the square there is a bird, perhaps an eagle.
82. Cubicle (12), wall E, section S below the window. The white plinth, divided into plinth and panels with a plan, is surmounted by a yellow frame.

83. Cubicle (12), S wall, section E, upper area. The panel of the middle area is bordered by a border of carpet with circumscribed palmettes. The frame between the middle and upper areas is adorned with lotuses and buds. The arched garland, in the center of which a bucket and a pedum are hung, is surmounted by a deer: an animal sacred to Dionysus that dresses in his skin (nebris), and to whose circle also belongs the crater placed on the epistyle.

Triclinium (16), N. wall On the white background of the wall is painted a deep aedicule with a high pluteus between the columns on both sides, with a coffered ceiling and a low tympanum with small acrotera, placed under a ceiling with a clypeus and hanging weapons. The central panel of the plinth is decorated with plants and a bird, between the two side panels with clypeus. The vignettes on the side panels of the middle area depict a rampant doe and a goat, those of the predella a bird in flight; the vignette in the aedicule depicts the attributes of Mercury.

86. Triclinium (16), back wall E. The central aedicule is flanked by architectural views with a tree; The vignette depicting a still life with fish in the center of the wall indicates the function of the room. The ceiling, almost completely reconstructed, is divided into a lowered vault flanked by platforms along the N and S walls. 80 N57504

87. Triclinium (16), S. The wall with a white background reflects the entire wall opposite, with the exception of the vignette in the center depicting the attributes of Minerva. In addition, there is the motif of the globe surmounted by an eagle preserved in the upper area, under the stucco frame with lotuses alternating with trefoils.

88. Triclinium (16), floor. The cocciopesto floor dating back to the late Republican era, indicates the place of the triclinium beds along the walls, around the canteen located in the middle. The ornamentation of the part occupied by the beds is limited to a regular dotting of crosses, composed of a black tile between four white tiles. The threshold takes up a coffered design: a row of squares with concave sides placed at an angle, each square with a cross in the center.

89. Triclinium (16), floor, section O, detail. The carpet under the table is polychrome mosaic; The cosmic significance of the circular table, and therefore of the motif that adorns the floor below, is well known. Here, the N-S axis of the circle is given by two thyrsis (dìthyrson: Anth. Pal., 6.172) with the usual red bandage, knotted under the green pine cone fixed to the tip of the javelin. 90. Triclinium (16), floor, section O, detail: the polychrome mosaic carpet.
91. Triclinium (16), N wall, W section, middle area, detail: vignette depicting a rampant doe in profile on the right.

92. Triclinium (16), N wall, central section, middle area, detail: vignette depicting the attributes of Mercury, the caduceus leaning on a small pillar, the rooster, the winged yellow hat (petasus) placed on a small column covered by a red cloak, at the foot of which stands a ram.

93. Triclinium (16), N wall, section E, middle area, detail: vignette depicting a rampant goat in profile on the left. The plastic effect of the lamps on the most protruding parts of the body is remarkable.

94. Triclinium (16), N wall, O section, predella. The bird flying to the right moves towards the center of the wall, like the doe in the panel above. The predella is bordered at the top by a red triangle carpet border.

Triclinium (16), wall E, central section, middle area, detail: vignette depicting a still life composed of edibles, which falls into the category of xenia, i.e. foods prepared for guests, often painted in the rooms intended for them (hospitalia) according to Vitruvius (De Arch., 6.7.4). Here it is an overturned basket, from which two wrasses and a mullet emerge in the foreground, a grouper, and two mullets.

96. Triclinium (16), E wall, S section, middle area, detail: vignette. The rampant panther depicted in profile on the left belongs to the Dionysian circle, as does the mystical cist veiled by a cloth painted in the upper area of the wall (fig. 86).

97. Triclinium (16), wall E, section S, predella. The vignette shows a bird flying to the left under the edge of a red triangle carpet, which delimits the predella at the top. Clearly visible is the not exactly straight horizontal line engraved in the fresh plaster to guide the painter's hand in the execution of the carpet edge.

98. Triclinium (16), S wall, E section, upper area. The globe surmounted by the eagle of Jupiter is supported by a winged female figure ending in shoots, with two plates in her hands raised at shoulder height. Similar anthropomorphic supports were widespread in Hellenistic and Roman toreutics. The reference to the lord of the cosmos, to whose daughter Minerva there is an allusion in the center of the wall, occurs naturally in the highest area of the wall. 80 N57512
99. Triclinium (16), S wall, section E, middle area, detail: vignette depicting a rampant doe in profile on the right.

101. Triclinium (16), S wall, central section, plinth. The panel arranged above a low plinth includes a series of plants with a bird in flight. In the aedicule above there is a floral candelabrum, the top of which is the meeting point of two garlands stretched in an arch. Note the darker strip of plaster in correspondence with the candelabra and garlands, determined by the pressure specially exerted before the application of the colors.

102. Triclinium (17), external S, section W seen from S-E. The exterior of the S-W pillar is decorated with a white background with carpet borders and swan flying towards the entrance. The headboard, built in opus listatum, was covered with a wooden jamb. On the left is visible the lararium of the corridor (18), with an arched niche.

The precious stained glass carpet below the table was covered with a sheet of lead. 49. Exedra (e), wall E, central section, middle area, detail: painting depicting Heracles (deceased) and Nessus. The centaur on his knees, his back covered by the pardalis knotted around his neck, offers himself to Heracles as the ferryman of Deianira, wife of Heracles and daughter of Dionysus. The gesture of the centaur indicates the depth of the waters. With her on his back, Nessus crosses the river and, having arrived on the other bank, tries to use violence against her; but it is struck in the chest by Heracles' arrow, shot from half a mile away. So he advises Deianira to wet Heracles' shirt in the well of blood and sperm poured on the ground, to ensure her husband's fidelity. But it is a poison that will cause the death and apotheosis of Heracles, assisted by his son Hyllus. In the painting appears the head of Deianira, who holds the little Hyllus to his chest in the chariot pulled by two horses. Behind the horses you can see a tree, a mountain (on the right) and a building (on the left). The other four older known replicas of the scene appear only in paintings of the III style of good quality: VI 9,3, (26): VIII 5,16, (b); IX 2:16, (e); IX 5:18, (g). The model was probably a painting by Artemon, a painter active in Asia Minor in the first half of the third century B.C. (Plin., Nat. hist., XXXV, 139). Veils, Maenads, pinakes and tripods depicted in the area above the painting, are initiatory tools; being hybrid, participating in human and animal nature, the Centaur is a mediator or bridge between two worlds. The wide gesture of the arms is surprising, identical to that of the Silenus Marsyas, another mediator between two levels, depicted in the alcove of the cubicle (f).  26 AFS C1527

54. Cubicle (f), alcove, wall E, central section, middle area, detail. On the hillock in the center of the Arcadian landscape seen from the arched window there is a pine tree (Arcadio pinus amat deo: Prop., EI., 1.18.20) and a column with a bandage. In front of the classical ithyphallic herm of Hermes (Mercury) with a stiff beard under the long wavy hair at the temples, there is a balcony with pomegranates offered by the cattleman with a hat and an empty sack under his arm, resting on the stick (incumbens tereti Damon... olivae: Verg., Buc., 8.16). He has his gaze lowered on the dog drinking in a puddle. On the high base at the back, the statue of Heracles seated with his right hand stretched out on the club contemplating the two oxen or grazing bulls of the cattleman. The painter has inverted the model of Lysippus' Herakles Epitrapèzios, which rests his left hand on the club. The landscape painter of I 7.19 seems to be also the author of the goat painted in the landscape of the painting of Dirce in the triclinium (EE) of the nearby House of C. Iulius Polybius (IX 13.3).
